title: Mixing households of different races in each block
issue: Has the rule that mixes races in every block been good for residents?
background:
Most people in Singapore live in public flats. Since 1989, a rule has set a limit on the share of flats in each block and each neighbourhood that households of one race may own. When a limit is reached, an owner may sell only to a buyer whose race will not push the share higher.

The rule is meant to stop any estate from becoming home to one race only, and to let neighbours of different races meet in daily life. Some owners say it makes their flats harder to sell. In 2024, residents of one estate were asked what they thought of the rule.

Study the sources to find out whether the rule has been good for residents.

sources.provenance: A poster by the housing authority, put up at bus stops in housing estates in 2024.
sources.text:
Look down your corridor.
One neighbour hangs lanterns for the Mid-Autumn Festival. Another lights oil lamps for Deepavali. A third brings round kuih for Hari Raya.
This did not happen by chance. In every block, families of every race live side by side, because the rule keeps it so.
Different doors. One corridor. That is home.

sources.provenance: A letter from a flat owner to the housing authority, written in 2024 after selling a flat in the estate.
sources.text: I put my flat up for sale last March. The limit for buyers of my own race had been reached in my block, so most of the families who came to view could not buy it. After nine months I sold to the only buyer allowed, for $38,000 less than a neighbour two floors up got the year before. My children grew up with friends of every race on this floor, and I am glad of it. But the whole country gains from mixed blocks, while the cost fell on my family alone.

sources.provenance: A resident who has lived in the estate for thirty years, interviewed for a neighbourhood newsletter.
sources.text: When I worked night shifts, the family next door took my son in after school every day. They are of a different race and religion from us. They never once gave him food he could not eat. Today my son and their daughter still meet for supper. If we had all lived among our own kind, I would have known them only as faces on a bus. Some people say the rule is a burden. For me it was the best thing that happened to this family.

sources.provenance: From a statement by a spokesperson for the housing authority, replying to questions from reporters in 2024.
sources.text: The rule has served residents well for more than thirty years. Every block in this estate is home to families of all races. Residents get along: nine in ten tell us they are comfortable with neighbours of another race. Only a very small number of sellers are affected by the limits, and any of them may appeal. The rule does not hold back prices. We see no reason to change it.

sources.provenance: From a study by university researchers, who surveyed 500 households in the estate in 2024.
sources.text: 86% of households said they were comfortable having neighbours of another race, and 71% greet such a neighbour most days. But only 22% had shared a meal with one in the past year. One block in three had reached a limit. In those blocks, flats took about four months longer to sell and went for about 5% less. Even so, 64% of the owners in those blocks said the rule should stay.

sources.provenance: A property agent who has sold flats in the estate for eleven years, writing in an online post.
sources.text: I have seen the rule hurt the same kind of owner again and again. A seller in a block at the limit has fewer buyers to choose from, and the buyers know it, so they bargain hard. Appeals are slow and most fail. And living next door does not make people friends. Many of my clients cannot name the family across the corridor. The rule mixes addresses. It cannot mix lives.

The message is that living beside neighbours of other races is something to be proud of, and that the rule on mixing is what makes it possible. The poster says 'This did not happen by chance' and that families of every race live side by side 'because the rule keeps it so'. This shows that the mixed corridor is the result of the rule and not of luck. The last line, 'Different doors. One corridor. That is home', makes the mix sound warm and normal. The poster is speaking to people who live in flats. It wants them to value their mixed block, so that they support the rule.

questions.question: Study Source D. How reliable is this source as evidence that the rule has been good for residents? Explain your answer.

seeded.text: Source D is reliable because it is a statement from the housing authority. The housing authority runs the rule, so it knows how the rule works.

Source D is reliable. It says 'Every block in this estate is home to families of all races' and 'nine in ten tell us they are comfortable with neighbours of another race'. These are clear facts, so it shows the rule has been good for residents.

Source D is only partly reliable. It says 'nine in ten tell us they are comfortable with neighbours of another race'. Source E supports this: '86% of households said they were comfortable having neighbours of another race'. But D also says 'Only a very small number of sellers are affected' and 'The rule does not hold back prices'. Source E found that 'One block in three had reached a limit', and that flats there 'went for about 5% less'. The owner in Source B sold for '$38,000 less'. The check shows that D is right about how neighbours feel but wrong about the cost to sellers. So it cannot be fully trusted as evidence that the rule has been good for residents.

questions.question: 'The rule that mixes races in every block has been good for residents.' Using the sources in this case study, explain how far you would agree with this statement.

seeded.text: I agree because it is good for people of different races to live together. Singapore has many races, so we should all mix.

Yet Source E, by researchers with no side to take, backs D on the main point: '86% of households said they were comfortable having neighbours of another race'. F is an agent who earns from sales, so the writer has a reason to dislike the limits, and the claim about friendship rests only on what clients say. B is one owner, but E backs the letter too: flats in blocks at a limit 'went for about 5% less'. E also shows that even there '64% of the owners in those blocks said the rule should stay'. So I agree to a large extent: the rule has made mixed living normal and most residents want to keep it, but its cost falls on a small group of sellers.
